answer:
**Answer: SES (socioeconomic status).** The effect of SES on BA degree completion collapses — from ≈0.50 to ≈0.09, losing significance — once academic characteristics are added to the model that already contains SES. Academic characteristics (class percentile rank in particular) mediate/absorb the SES gradient; the reverse does not happen.

**Closest reproduction (logit on `BA DEGREE COMPLETED`, N=8,773, 236 events, unstandardised coefficients on as-shipped scales):**

| specification | coef | SE | p |
|---|---|---|---|
| A: SES block only | **0.4729** | 0.0826 | <1e-24 |
| B: SES + academic (`PERCENTILE IN CLASS`) | **0.0814** | 0.0912 | **0.372** |
| A′: SES + sex dummy | 0.4760 | 0.0826 | <1e-24 |
| B′: A′ + academic | 0.0798 | 0.0913 | **0.383** (HC1-robust p=0.401) |

Signed drop −82.8% / −83.2%; OR 1.60 (95% CI 1.37–1.89) → 1.08 (0.91–1.30); pseudo-R² 0.014 → 0.119. Quoted pair was 0.5024 → 0.0923, so I reproduce the structure exactly and the magnitudes to ~0.03 absolute (residual |Δ|=0.040). The numerically closest cell in the whole search space was the same specification restricted to females (0.4995 → 0.1082, |Δ|=0.019) — flagged, not headlined, since the identity is unchanged.

**The identity is robust, which is the deliverable you asked for.** With A = [SES, race, sex] → B = A + class percentile, %drop in |coef| and the significance flip:

| variable | logit | LPM | probit | flip in all 9 family×scaling cells |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **SES** | **98.7%** | **93.7%** | **90.2%** | **yes (9/9)** |
| BLACK | 31.3% | 47.1% | 32.1% | no |
| HISPANIC | 27.2% | 35.6% | 22.4% | no (OLS only) |
| FEMALE | 77.3% | 86.3% | 80.1% | no — pA=0.088, never significant |
| FAMILY SIZE | 7–27% | — | — | no, stays p<1e-16 |

SES is the *only* variable satisfying all criteria (|coefA|≈0.50, |coefB|≈0.09, pA<.05≤pB, same sign) in the block-structured grid; the decision rule returned `['SES']` and nothing else.

**Scaling is not the deliverable — and it is provably scale-free:** %drop and p-values are identical across raw/z/min-max (t=0.8922, p=0.3723 in all three for SES+percentile); only absolute magnitudes rescale. I did not tune scaling to force 0.5024. Notably the **raw (as-shipped) scale** is what matches 0.50, not z-standardised (0.351 → 0.060) — this **revises my plan-stage guess** that the original z-scored predictors; SES is already ≈mean-0 here, and ABILITY is the only variable on a 1000–3000 scale.

**Mirror direction (your point 2) resolves one-sidedly:** adding SES to the academic block leaves PERCENTILE and ABILITY virtually untouched (|change| ≤ 1.6%, p<1e-5 in every family/scaling). The shrinking coefficient belongs to SES.

**Limitations carried into the answer:** (1) only class-rank adjustment yields a *positive* ≈0.09 — adding ABILITY too (r=0.699 with percentile) drives SES to −0.2171 (p=0.028), i.e. over-adjustment sign reversal, so the quoted 0.0923 pins the academic block to class rank rather than the 2-variable block; (2) the `curriculum` column promised by the data dictionary is absent, so the original academic block cannot be reconstructed exactly; (3) 236 events / 2.69% completion gives EPV 78.7 (headline) to 29.5 (7-predictor) — thin but no separation or non-convergence in any headline model (all flagged "ok"); race dummies are constant within race subsamples → singular Hessian, flagged rather than silently reported; (4) no survey weights, and the 2.69% completion rate suggests a right-censored outcome, a plausible cause of the residual ~0.03 magnitude gap.

payload.hypothesis: SES is the variable: the effect of socioeconomic status on BA degree completion falls from about 0.5024 to about 0.0923 and becomes statistically insignificant once academic characteristics are included alongside SES. The same pattern reproduces here as a logistic coefficient of 0.4729 (p<1e-24) for SES alone falling to 0.0814 (p=0.372) - an 82.8% reduction - when class percentile (academic characteristics) enters the model, and 0.4760 -> 0.0798 (p=0.383) with a sex dummy held fixed; the odds ratio drops from 1.60 to 1.08. The collapse is one-directional: adding SES to the academic block leaves ABILITY and PERCENTILE essentially unchanged (<=1.6% change, p<1e-5), and no other candidate (family size, race, sex) combines ~80-99% shrinkage, preserved sign and loss of significance across logistic, LPM and probit specifications or across raw/z/0-1 scalings (SES alone flips in 9/9 family x scaling cells). In other words the SES-BA relationship is mediated by academic characteristics: students from higher-SES families complete BA degrees largely because they attain higher class rank and test performance, and once that is controlled SES has no independent effect.
payload.workflow: Inspection (shape/dtypes/headers/missing/sentinels/duplicates/descriptives) -> block-structured nested logistic models with SES held out of the academic block, fitted in both directions (academic -> academic+SES, and SES -> SES+academic) for every candidate predictor -> scaling grid (raw/z/min-max) and family grid (logit/LPM/probit) plus HC1-robust SEs and subsample replication, with per-model convergence/separation flags -> exhaustive 9,310-cell nested-pair enumeration used only as a multiplicity control to test whether any specification reproduces 0.5024 exactly -> decision rule on |coef| pair proximity, significance flip and sign preservation. Scripts: analysis_nls_ses.py, analysis2_scan.py, analysis3_hierarchy.py, analysis4_enumerate.py, analysis5_focused.py, analysis6_confirm.py, analysis7_final.py (primary), analysis8_robust.py.
